content_voiceover: This table lines up WHO and ICC classification side by side against the same clinical inputs, blast counts, cytogenetics, and mutations, which is a great way to cross check your understanding before boards. For marrow blasts under 5 percent and blood under 2 percent, a 5 q deletion gives MDS dash 5 q under WHO and MDS dash 5 q under ICC, essentially the same label. An S F 3 B 1 mutation gives MDS dash S F 3 B 1 under both systems. Other genetic profiles in this low blast group give MDS dash L B under WHO, which maps to MDS N O S without dysplasia or with single or multilineage dysplasia under ICC. For marrow blasts 5 to 9 percent with blood 2 to 4 percent, WHO calls this MDS dash I B 1, while ICC calls the same range MDS dash E B. For marrow blasts 10 to 19 percent with blood 5 to 19 percent, WHO calls this MDS dash I B 2, and ICC calls it MDS slash AML. Running across the top of both systems, biallelic T P 53 under WHO becomes MDS dash bi T P 53, and under ICC becomes MDS dash T P 53, and cases with fibrosis get MDS dash f under WHO regardless of blast count. The highlighted orange row emphasizes that when AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality criteria are met at the 10 to 19 percent blast range, ICC labels the case MDS slash AML or AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality, while the T P 53 column separately captures MDS dash T P 53 or AML dash T P 53 depending on blast percentage.
keypoints: Low blast group: MDS dash 5q and MDS dash S F 3 B 1 labels align closely between WHO and ICC
WHO MDS dash L B corresponds to ICC MDS N O S subtypes
5 to 9 percent blasts: WHO I B 1 equals ICC MDS dash E B
10 to 19 percent blasts: WHO I B 2 equals ICC MDS slash AML
Biallelic or mutated T P 53 tracks separately across both systems at any blast count
keypoint_voiceover: Use this table as your quick conversion chart. The biggest naming differences appear at higher blast counts, where WHO uses I B 1 and I B 2 based purely on percentage, while ICC uses MDS dash E B and MDS slash AML, and also carves out a separate AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormality pathway that WHO does not use in quite the same way.
